'''''Euphorbia caput-medusae''''' ("'''Medusa's Head'''") is a plant of the genus ''[[Euphorbia]]'' that occurs in and around [[Cape Town]], [[South Africa]].

==Description==
This succulent resembles the head of Medusa, with many serpent-like stems arising from a short, central caudex. They sometimes exceed {{Convert|1|m}} in diameter, partly buried in the ground, covered with numerous crowded branches.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantefg/euphorbia.htm | title=Euphorbia | PlantZAfrica.com}}</ref>

''Euphorbia caput-medusae'' was introduced to the Netherlands around 1700 and was one of the early plants described by Linnaeus (''[[Species Plantarum]]'', 1753).<ref name="Kew">{{cite web|url=http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Euphorbia-caput-medusae.htm|title=Euphorbia caput-medusae (Medusa's head)|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date=1 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120518000518/http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Euphorbia-caput-medusae.htm|archive-date=18 May 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Distribution==
This species is primarily coastal, occurring along the western coast of [[South Africa]], southwards to the [[Cape Peninsula]]. 
It is still common around [[Cape Town]] where it grows in deep sand or rocky outcrops on the coast. It is particularly common in the [[Peninsula Shale Renosterveld]] vegetation of [[Signal Hill (Cape Town)|Signal Hill]]. 

It also occurs along the south coast of the [[Western Cape Province]], from Cape Town the form previously known as ''muirii'' extends along the coast eastwards as far as [[Mossel Bay]].<ref>Goldblatt, P. & Manning, J. (2000) ''Cape Plants. A Conspectus of the Cape Flora of South Africa.'' SANBI, Cape Town & Missouri Botanical Garden, St Louis.</ref>
